Introduction
Exporting copper busbars to the US and EU requires more than good manufacturing — it demands compliance with international standards, proper documentation, and logistics planning.
This guide explains everything from customs classification (HS codes) and tariff duties to certifications like RoHS, REACH, and UL, helping suppliers like Wellgo Battery ship efficiently while meeting all regulatory requirements.
Understand the Product: What Counts as a Copper Busbar
Copper busbars are conductive strips or bars used for power distribution in EV battery systems, energy storage, and industrial equipment.
● Under the Harmonized System (HS), most busbars fall under:HS Code: 7407.21 — Bars, rods, and profiles of refined copper.
● Alternate: 8538.90 — Parts suitable for electrical apparatus or battery connectors.
Wellgo Battery exports custom copper-nickel busbars optimized for EV batteries and ESS modules, aligning with each destination’s import classification to reduce customs risks.
Reference: Harmonized Tariff Schedule | EU TARIC Database
Check Export Tariffs and Import Duties
The tariff rate varies by region and trade policy:
| Destination | HS Code | Base Tariff | Notes | 
| United States | 7407.21 | 0–2.5% | Copper busbars under “industrial use” are often duty-free under USITC | 
| European Union | 7407.21 | 0% | Under EU customs union; import VAT applies (19–23%) | 
| UK (Post-Brexit) | 7407.21 | 0–1.5% | Separate customs declaration required | 
Wellgo Battery maintains tariff documentation to ensure transparent pricing for global clients and leverages preferential trade agreements to reduce costs where applicable.
Ensure Compliance with RoHS and REACH Regulations
The EU and US both enforce strict rules on hazardous substances and material traceability:
● ", "title": "Export Guide: Shipping Copper Busbars to the US and EU", "url": "https://wellgobattery.myshopify.com/et/blogs/industry-news-battery-connector-solutions/export-guide-copper-busbars-us-eu", "publisher_type": "secondary_or_unverified_publisher", "retrieved_at": "2026-09-09T16:51:34.627237+00:00"}, {"passage_id": "passage_c8c4aa7f130dba0d3c42316c", "chunk_id": "chunk_d625c75d6d3fc6f5cf2f6a0a", "document_id": "document_78d5f38ea11227317f5a972a", "text": " Chinese manufacturers absorbed cost pressure through aggressive pricing strategies aimed at maintaining market share in export markets. For US OEMs sourcing domestically compliant supply chains, the experience was sharply negative.
The Materials Most Affected
| Material / Component | Tariff Rate | Battery Pack Impact | Availability of US Alternatives | 
| Chinese graphite (anode) | 93.5% | Directly raises cell cost | Very limited – US production minimal | 
| Chinese lithium-ion cells | 30%+ baseline | Core pack component affected | Growing – Korean, Japanese options | 
| Steel (housings, brackets) | 50% | Enclosure and structural costs | Yes – US steel available at premium | 
| Copper (busbars, wiring) | 50% | Electrical interconnects, connectors | Yes – US and Chilean sources | 
| Chinese PCBs and BMS | 25–30% | Electronics in smart battery packs | Moderate – Taiwan, Korea options | 
| Cobalt (NMC cathodes) | Variable by origin | Premium chemistry packs | Congo export quotas add further risk | 
 
Totex Perspective: The tariff impact is not uniform across all battery pack types. Custom battery packs with US-engineered BMS, domestically sourced housings, and Korean or Japanese cells have significantly lower tariff exposure than packs built entirely from Chinese components. The key is understanding your exact bill of materials and tracing every component’s country of origin. Our engineering team performs this analysis as part of every program review.
 
3. How the US Battery Supply Chain Is Shifting
The tariff environment is accelerating structural changes in battery supply chains that were already underway. Understanding these shifts is essential for OEMs making long-term sourcing decisions in 2026 and beyond.
Reshoring and Nearshoring Momentum

Every battery pack includes plastic housing, lithium-ion cells, cell brackets, nickel or copper sheets that connect the cells, electric wires, insulation and protection material, and terminals. Each pack also contains a battery management system, composed of a printed circuit board assembly (“PCBA”) and electronic components, which runs software and coordinates and monitors the electric flow between the lithium-ion cells and compatible tools also manufactured by Greenworks Tools.  The lithium-ion cells are designed to store and provide power to the power tools with DC power.  When combined with a compatible power tool, the battery pack provides power to the tool through the positive and negative poles, and there is a communication interface which is used to connect the communication between the battery management system and the tool.

2.2 Product Description Alone Is Not Enough
Voltage, capacity, chemistry, enclosure, intended use, included charger, and whether components are imported together can affect classification. In a March 2026 CBP ruling, a rechargeable 3.7V, 1150mAh lithium-ion replacement battery for a noise-canceling headset was classified under HTSUS 8507.60.0090. This example is useful, but a CBP ruling applies to the merchandise described in that ruling and should not automatically be extended to a different pack.
When classification uncertainty could materially change duty, importers may consult a customs professional or request a binding ruling from U.S. Customs and Border Protection.
2.3 Cells, Battery Packs, Chargers, and Host Devices May Differ
A shipment described commercially as a “battery solution” may contain several legally distinct items:
- Lithium-ion cells
- Assembled battery packs
- BMS or PCM assemblies
- AC/DC chargers and adapters
- Battery cables, connectors, and accessories
- A battery installed in or packed with equipment
Classification for customs duty is separate from dangerous-goods classification. UN 3480 and UN 3481 determine how lithium-ion batteries are described and handled for transport, but they do not replace the HTS classification used to calculate import duty. See our guide to UN 3480 vs UN 3481 for the transport distinction.

1. Impact of Battery Tariffs Across Energy Sectors
Recent trade adjustments have introduced significant increases in battery tariffs, ranging from 54% to 104%, depending on product type and classification. These duties now apply to a broad range of products, including:
- Grid-scale lithium-ion batteries used in solar and wind energy storage projects
- EV battery components, including cells, modules, and upstream materials
